i disagree--they were packed up front and then not really mentioned again. free solo is structured so those moments play out with the climb as well. dawn wall was very much: "this happened, and moving on, a climb." the story could've interlaced those experience throughout, or drawn a more clear connection to the dawn wall.

for example, in his book, tommy caldwell has said he initially wanted to free solo el cap because “if i took away the rope, the experience would be that much stronger. that much more real…and if i fell to my death, at least the pain would be gone, too.” instead he fights that pull, reconnects with the dawn wall and works after that. in the film, they skip over the whole suicidal part and only allude to the depression as "well, it was there and i needed to get out of the house." there was the opportunity much stronger emotional arc than free solo but they way they structured the narrative killed that momentum.

hey guys, so i figured i would get some feedback and talk about deciding to compete. this forum is a home for me, and i used other people’s post as a source of information before deciding to compete.

i started off in powerlifting (525 squat, 405 bench, 635 dl) at my college and wanted to shred down for the summer as i successfully winter bulked myself to 215 pounds at 5’8”. i knew how to run my own macros and diet down successfully but decided to get a coach who might be more aggressive than i would with myself. the coach is our ugly big-headed egg master, goob ([http://www.instagram.com/goob\_u](http://www.instagram.com/goob_u)). long story short, the cut was going well, and i was happy. goob suggested i could compete and do well, if i wanted. i mulled over it for a few weeks, asking my friends what they thought, and everyone said i should do it. so, i was like “fuck it, lets go! i have watched some guys in prep and yea it sucks but it’s not that bad”. i was wrong, but it has been one of the most rewarding experience.

we are on week 16 of this prep and i’m not going to lie, it sucks. i’m drained and tired of dieting. i eat a lot of egg whites, chicken and veggies. walden farms and mustard has kept my sanity as my carbs seemingly go down the drain every week. cardio is around 45 minutes per day. i am friends with the treadmill and stairmaster, but my knees have taken a toll, so i mix the bike in a few times a week. as of now, i’m sitting around 185 (5’8”) and the class limit is 190.

the mental sides (for me) are the worst. i binged around 4-5 times this prep early in the prep. i have much better control of it now. my coping mechanism is watching youtube videos of other people eating foods i think sound good (donuts and pizza, mostly). i did time in the army (airborne and army ranger) and go to a decent school but prepping for a competition (while trying to do midterms) is possibly just as hard as anything else i have done so far. i’m not bitching but this truly tests your mental will (especially when you have other responsibilities). needless to say, i love the challenge. thanks r/bb for being a home for us all.

it’s easy to get caught into body dysmorphia at a young age. i’ve been in the same boat, i looked at guys like zyzz, steve cook etc as guys who had my dream physiques. no matter how much i trained or how muscley i became i was never satisfied. it’s becomes a mental illness

i backed off that and trained purely for athletics and was more satisfied and content with myself being able to put data to my results in the form of strength training, sprint times, vertical jumps, flexibility etc and the funny thing is, looking back at photos of myself from 5-6 years ago, i actually had a physique then at the time that i would have looked at when i was 18 and said “that’s a dream physique” but while i had it, i never noticed it and actually felt more insecure about my weight at 8% body fat than i do now at 15%, and always wanted more

it’s a double edged sword. i would recommend using these guys as an inspiration for what is possible, but you don’t need to look like these guys. the guy you linked is a bit of a specimen, a david laid lite if you will. train for what will make you happy and content and remember this is something you will do for maybe the next 30 years of your life. your goals and perspectives will change every few years, and something you worked your hardest to achieve in 5 years, might be something you hate in 10 years time.

train with an open mind, dont get too caught up on aesthetics, the guys we see on instagram / magazines / tv etc are the top 0.01% of this lifestyle. they get paid to do it, they take supplements and peds to achieve the results in some cases

if you look around your local environment and see people who you deem look good or have an ideal physique, use that as your measure instead, because it’s a much more realistic view of being healthy and having a nice physique

girls or guys don’t exclusively go for men that look like the instagram models, and that’s simply because they exist in an extremely limited supply. get strong, build muscle, have a healthy lifestyle, be capable of doing what you want to achieve with your body and be confident. that’s a happier goal to achieve (for me atleast)

what i’ve been working on lately is changing the way i deal with fear.

many see fear as something to be conquered or overcome, but i’m a sensitive soul and i just don’t do well being at war with myself. i treat my fear gently and lovingly. i ask it what it’s afraid of, and why.

like, if i was afraid of loose skin and stretch marks, i would let myself think of those things and let myself be scared of them, without judging myself for having those feelings. and knowing it’s just me here, and i’m not gonna judge me, my fear can be honest. i can sit with it a while and it will finally say: i am afraid too much damage has already been done. i am afraid that i would have to deal with loose skin and stretch marks, but have nothing to show for it. (not trying to put thoughts in your head here! i’m just projecting my own feelings here as an example.)

every single time i ask my fear “why?,” the answer always comes back “i am trying to keep you safe.” in this case, if my fear truly believed that the damage was already done, wouldn’t it be safer to not have the stress of the way my skin looks on top of that? i like to think that my fear loves me and wants me to be safe.  so i love my fear (and myself) back by allowing it to be felt and validated.

now i am at a point where my fear will respond to rationality. i mean, i’m a lot more likely to hear someone out when they have heard me out first and told me my concerns were valid, y’know? so now (and still releasing any judgments that come up!) i can ask my fear something like “how do i feel now? do i think eating well and working out has had a positive or negative effect? if i feel better now than i did 3 months ago, could it be possible that my body is improving?”

if you’re like me, your fear might say, “well... i am less depressed... and i sure do like these muscles...”

at which point i can gently ask, “would it really be safer to stay out of shape?”

for me, anyway, this is the second step to challenging my own fears and limiting beliefs. (awareness is the first!) i also like to do affirmations, which i know many find super cheesy. they’re amazing for me, though!

i'm a therapist and do a lot of work with ptsd/abuse type stuff. i almost exclusively use emdr to work on these things.  
  
couple thoughts: my guess is you've successfully distracted yourself from a lot of this for a long time. but with swimming, there is less to distract you. unless you spend a lot of money for a music streaming system, it is just you and your thoughts.  
  
emdr therapy is thought to work in part through the "bilateral stimulation" of stimulating the left and right hemispheres of your brain alternatively, back and forth back and forth. therapists typically use eye movements or other forms of bilateral stimulation such as tones in headphones or buzzers held in your hands. but lots of other things are also bilateral. such as swimming, running/walking and so on.  
  
so you may be experiencing a combination of the reduced opportunity of distraction with the bilateral stimulation that is causing this to come up.  
  
if you're comfortable with it and have good coping skills to utilize in case something really upsetting comes up, you may find that over time if you let yourself notice the throughts/feeligns/etc that come up while swimming, that much of it will naturally resolve over time.  
  
if you're not, then i would suggest finding something to distract yourself, such as music or counting or really focusing on technique. and also find an emdr therapist to work on that stuff that is coming up, so that it won't continue to intrude upon your life!
